vignette: He stands in the center of a concrete cell, thirty-eight years old, wrists bound, listening to boots echo down a narrow corridor. The air is thick with rust and stale sweat. For months, his days blur into a rhythm of forced labor, thin rations, and the constant, low hum of survival. He learns to make himself small, to sleep with one eye open, to keep his shoulders curled inward against the walls. When the men finally cut his restraints and point toward a border crossing, the sky feels too wide, the light too harsh. He does not look back. He crosses on foot, leaves his workshop and his steady wrenches behind, and begins the slow work of rebuilding his name in a new country, then in a new town, then in a house with heavy deadbolts. Decades pass. The plumbing business he rebuilt becomes his anchor. For thirty years, his hands know the language of pipes and pressure. He traces leaks through drywall, listens to water flow through copper, fixes what is broken with a patient's patience. Water is a medium he understands. Then, at sixty-nine, retirement arrives like an unspooled cable. The sudden quiet of his own home presses against his ribs. When the basement pipes groan at night, he lies awake, listening past the metallic sighs for the click of a boot on the stairwell. He checks the foundation door three times. He tells his wife, Mei, it is just the house settling. She stops asking questions. Her silence is heavier than his. He still sets the table with two pairs of chopsticks and a small bowl of jasmine rice, though he eats little. The scent of damp earth from the garden pulls him back to the provinces he left behind. He reaches for Mei's hand at dinner, but his fingers curl inward. He is afraid his calluses will crack her skin, afraid he will not remember how to hold anything without first gripping it. The neighbor's sprinkler triggers a memory of a drainage trench. He stands abruptly, knocking his teacup to the floor. The shatter echoes through the kitchen. Mei rushes in. He breathes through his nose, in for four, out for six. His jaw aches. He does not tell her about the dream where the walls close in, where he waits for a door that will not open. He picks up the ceramic shards one by one, measures the gaps between them, sweeps them into the bin. His body moves slower now, but the alertness does not fade. He scans the driveway when a delivery van approaches. He measures room safety in sightlines and exit paths. He still waters the hydrangeas Mei planted, his thumb brushing each leaf, counting them the way he used to count pipe joints. The past does not leave him; it lives in the space between his shoulders, in the way he pauses before stepping into an elevator, in the way he watches his wife's reflection in the microwave door. He sits back down in his recliner as the kettle begins its slow whistle. The rain traces the window. He waits. He listens. He stays.
